Women, sexual minority respondents, and White respondents reported higher odds across all four outcomes than their peers, and the researchers found further differences at the intersections of race, sex and sexual orientation. One important limitation: these are separate cross-sectional snapshots, not the same people followed over time, so the study can show that the young adult population looks more anxious than it did in 2020, but not why, and rising diagnosis and medication numbers can partly reflect better recognition and access rather than more illness.

title: Do anti-stigma trainings for doctors and nurses actually work?
blurb: Pooling 21 randomized controlled trials, educational anti-stigma programs modestly reduced healthcare workers' negative attitudes toward people with mental illness right after training (SMD = -0.38). Knowledge and willingness to be near patients did not improve, and the attitude gains were not maintained at follow-up.
summary: Hospitals and universities run a lot of anti-stigma workshops, and this review asked whether they change anything. The authors searched five research databases through July 2025 and pulled together every randomized controlled trial that tested an educational program aimed at reducing mental health stigma among healthcare professionals or students in training. Nineteen reports covering 21 studies made the cut. Immediately after training, participants scored meaningfully lower on explicit negative attitudes toward people with mental illness, with a pooled effect size of -0.38 (a small-to-moderate difference). Practicing clinicians also reported stronger intentions to behave differently, though students did not. But the picture gets thinner from there. Mental health knowledge did not improve. Neither did 'social distance,' the measure of how comfortable someone is living or working near a person with mental illness. And where studies followed up weeks or months later, the early gains had faded. The honest limitation is one the authors flag themselves: using the GRADE system, the certainty of the evidence ranged from very low to moderate, the trials used inconsistent outcome measures, and most looked only at what people said on a questionnaire, not at how they actually treated patients.

title: Does cannabis actually calm you down?
blurb: In a double-blind trial, 120 regular cannabis users vaped placebo, 20 mg THC, or 40 mg THC. Self-reported stress dropped about equally in all three groups, while heart rate rose significantly more on the high dose than on placebo.
summary: Stress relief is one of the most common reasons people give for using cannabis. This trial put that belief to a controlled test, and it is the first to track several stress systems at once. Researchers randomly assigned 120 regular cannabis users (56 men, 52 women, 12 non-binary or transgender participants) to vape one of three things without knowing which: placebo, a moderate 20 mg dose of THC, or a high 40 mg dose. Neither participants nor the researchers running the session knew the assignment. Stress ratings and saliva cortisol were collected before vaping, five minutes after, and an hour after, while a wristband continuously logged heart rate, heart rate variability, and skin conductance. The subjective result is the striking one: people reported feeling less stressed after vaping, but so did the placebo group, and by about the same amount, which points to expectancy rather than the drug. Physiologically, the picture split apart. Cortisol dropped more sharply on the high dose, and skin conductance responses dampened in both cannabis groups, but heart rate rose more on the high dose than on placebo. A key limitation: participants were all regular users tested in a lab, so this says little about occasional users or real-world stressful moments.

title: Can one day of an inhaled psychedelic lift treatment-resistant depression?
blurb: In a phase 2b trial across 16 European sites, 81 adults with treatment-resistant depression received up to three escalating inhaled doses of mebufotenin (GH001) or placebo on a single day. One week later, 57.5% of the drug group (23 of 40) were in remission, compared with 0% of the 41 placebo patients.
summary: Most people with treatment-resistant depression have already tried several antidepressants without much relief, so researchers keep looking for something that works faster and differently. This trial tested GH001, a synthetic inhaled form of mebufotenin (also known as 5-MeO-DMT, a short-acting psychedelic). Eighty-one adults aged 18 to 64 who had not responded to two to five previous antidepressants were randomly assigned, double-blind, to receive either GH001 or a matching placebo. Everything happened on a single day: participants got an individualized regimen of up to three escalating doses (6, 12, and 18 mg), then were followed for a week. On the standard depression rating scale, the GH001 group improved by about 15.5 points more than placebo, an unusually large effect. By day 8, 23 of 40 GH001 patients met the threshold for remission, while none of the 41 placebo patients did. No severe or serious adverse events were reported during the placebo-controlled period. The honest limitation: this is a small, one-week trial, and a drug that produces a vivid psychedelic experience is very hard to blind, so participants likely guessed which group they were in. The trial was also funded by the company developing the drug, and several authors are employees or shareholders. Longer, larger trials will decide whether the effect holds up.

title: Do antidepressants in pregnancy raise a child's risk of autism or ADHD?
blurb: A meta-analysis pooled 37 studies covering 648,626 antidepressant-exposed pregnancies and 24,967,806 unexposed ones. Raw estimates showed 35% higher ADHD risk and 69% higher autism risk in exposed children, but the associations shrank or disappeared once confounding was accounted for, and fathers' antidepressant use during pregnancy showed a similar pattern.
summary: This is one of the most common worries in perinatal psychiatry: is it safe to stay on an antidepressant while pregnant? Researchers searched four databases through May 2025 and pooled 37 studies comparing children born after prenatal antidepressant exposure with children who were not exposed, covering roughly 650,000 exposed and 25 million unexposed pregnancies. At first glance, the numbers look worrying: exposed children had about 35% higher relative risk of ADHD and 69% higher relative risk of autism. But the team then pushed on those numbers. Higher doses were not linked to higher autism risk. Exposure before conception, when the drug could not have reached the fetus, showed similar associations. And in the study's clever check, fathers' antidepressant use during pregnancy was also tied to more ADHD and autism in the children, which points toward shared family, genetic, and illness-related explanations rather than the medication itself. In analyses that adjusted for maternal mental illness and familial factors, most associations weakened or lost significance, and no specific SSRI or SNRI stood out. The authors rated the certainty of evidence as low to very low, and note that observational data can never fully rule out confounding. Their stated interpretation is that antidepressant treatment should continue for pregnant women with moderate-to-severe depression.

title: Does a parent's depression drag down a kid's grades?
blurb: Researchers tracked about 9,000 families in the Norwegian Mother, Father, and Child Study and compared cousins to strip out shared family background. Small links between parents' psychiatric symptoms and children's 5th-grade test scores disappeared once cousins were compared.
summary: It is a familiar assumption that a parent's anxiety, depression, ADHD, eating disorder, or drinking problem will show up in their child's report card. This study asked whether that link is actually causal. Using roughly 9,000 families from the large Norwegian Mother, Father, and Child Study, researchers had parents report their own symptoms during pregnancy and again during the child's childhood. The children then took Norway's nationally standardized 5th-grade tests in math, reading comprehension, and English at about age 10. The clever part is the design: instead of comparing unrelated families, the team compared children who are cousins, so that everything siblings-turned-parents share (genes, upbringing, neighborhood, social class) is held constant. In the ordinary analysis, more parental symptoms went with slightly lower reading and math scores, but the effects were tiny, with standardized betas between -0.060 and -0.013. In the cousin comparison, those associations were no longer statistically significant. The authors read this as evidence that parental symptoms do not directly move a child's achievement much on their own. One honest limitation: the families who could be included in the cousin analysis differed from the full sample, so the results may not generalize cleanly to all families, and the design cannot rule out very small effects.

title: Pesticides in pregnancy and autism traits: a big study finds no link
blurb: Researchers measured organophosphate pesticide breakdown products in the urine of 3,339 pregnant women across 20 US sites and later scored their children's autism-related traits. After full adjustment, prenatal exposure showed no association with those traits.
summary: Organophosphate pesticides are known neurotoxins, and most Americans get low-level exposure through food, so the worry that prenatal exposure might contribute to autism has circulated for years with inconsistent evidence behind it. This analysis pooled harmonized data from 20 study sites in the US ECHO cohort, following mother-child pairs recruited between 1997 and 2019. Scientists measured two markers of organophosphate exposure in the mothers' urine during pregnancy: TCPy and the sum of six dialkyl phosphate metabolites. Years later, parents rated their children on the Social Responsiveness Scale, a standard measure of autism-related traits, at an average age of 6.4 years. Among the 3,339 pairs, crude models actually hinted at slightly lower autism trait scores with higher exposure, but once the researchers adjusted for maternal demographics, behavior, and diet, the associations shrank to nothing, for example a beta of -0.13 (95% CI -0.57 to 0.31) per doubling of TCPy. Results held across boys and girls and across several alternative statistical approaches, and diet quality did not change the picture. Limitations worth noting: exposure came from spot urine samples, which reflect recent intake rather than a whole pregnancy, autism traits were parent-reported rather than clinically diagnosed, and the exposure range studied was typical dietary levels, not occupational ones.

title: Can a self-paced online program treat PTSD from childhood trauma?
blurb: 181 adults with PTSD linked to childhood interpersonal trauma tried an online program combining self-guided modules with optional virtual group sessions. It beat standard care on symptom reduction, with benefits still holding four months later.
summary: Adults whose PTSD traces back to childhood abuse or other interpersonal trauma often struggle to access specialized treatment, especially outside major cities. This trial tested "Trauma PORTAL," a hybrid program combining eight self-paced online psychoeducation and skills modules with eight optional one-hour virtual group sessions led by trauma therapists. Researchers in Ontario, Canada randomly assigned 181 adults (81% women, average age 41) with PTSD from childhood interpersonal trauma to either Trauma PORTAL or standard care. After eight weeks, the program group's PTSD symptoms (measured on the PCL-5 scale) had dropped about 7 points more than the standard-care group, a moderate effect, and that gap held steady at the 16-week follow-up. No adverse events were reported. The main limitation is that this was a single site with an assessor-blind but not participant-blind design, and it compared the program to routine care rather than to an existing gold-standard trauma therapy, so it shows the approach works better than doing nothing in particular, not that it matches specialized in-person treatment.

title: Bipolar Disorder May Rewire the Brain's Communication Network
blurb: Scans of 449 people with bipolar disorder and 510 controls across 16 sites found less efficient, more roundabout brain wiring in emotion and reward circuits, with the disruption tracking illness duration and severity.
summary: Using diffusion MRI, which maps the brain's white-matter wiring, an international team examined structural connectivity in 449 people diagnosed with bipolar disorder and 510 healthy controls across 16 research sites worldwide, coordinated through the ENIGMA Bipolar Disorder Working Group. Rather than looking at single brain regions, they modeled the brain as a network and measured how efficiently different regions communicate with each other. People with bipolar disorder showed less densely connected networks, longer communication paths between regions, and greater reliance on a small number of 'hub' regions to relay signals -- changes concentrated in circuits tied to emotion regulation, reward processing, and memory, including connections between the amygdala, hippocampus, and frontal cortex. These network disruptions were more pronounced in people with longer illness duration, later age of first episode, and a history of psychosis, while a higher number of past manic episodes was linked to unexpectedly stronger connectivity in some emotion-related circuits. Common medications, including antidepressants, anticonvulsants, and antipsychotics, were associated with reduced connectivity in some circuits, though the effect of lithium was unclear. Because the study captured each person's brain at a single point in time rather than tracking them over years, the researchers can't say whether these network changes cause worsening symptoms, result from them, or simply reflect medication exposure -- only that they travel together.

title: Do more risk genes mean more severe schizophrenia?
blurb: Researchers compared 346 people hospitalized continuously for at least five years with treatment-resistant schizophrenia against more than 18,000 others. Each standard-deviation rise in schizophrenia polygenic score raised the odds of being in that most severe group by 40% to 80%.
summary: More than one in five people with schizophrenia get little or no benefit from antipsychotic medication, and a smaller group stays severely ill for years on end. Researchers asked whether that most severe form carries a heavier load of the common genetic variants linked to schizophrenia. They recruited 346 people of European ancestry from Pennsylvania state psychiatric hospitals who met a strict definition: at least five years of continuous hospitalization, active treatment, and no response to three or more antipsychotics. They compared them with 10,757 people with treatment-resistant schizophrenia, 1,148 with schizophrenia generally, and 6,320 people without psychiatric diagnoses, drawn from cohorts in the US, Sweden, and the UK, for 18,571 people in total. For each standard-deviation increase in schizophrenia polygenic score, the odds of being in the continuously hospitalized group rose by 40% to 80% relative to the other schizophrenia groups. A smaller exploratory analysis in 476 people of African ancestry (78 cases) pointed in the same direction with weaker statistical support. The pattern held after accounting for sex and after excluding people with additional diagnoses. Limits worth naming: the comparison groups came from different countries and recruitment settings, which can introduce differences that have nothing to do with genetics; the effect describes group averages rather than any individual's prognosis; and polygenic scores still perform poorly outside European-ancestry samples.

title: A Polish Version of the 'Dark Tetrad' Test Mostly Holds Up, With One Weak Spot
blurb: A 931-person validation of the Polish Short Dark Tetrad found the sadism and psychopathy scales performed well, but the Machiavellianism subscale showed weak internal reliability (alpha = .67).
summary: The Short Dark Tetrad (SD4) is a brief 28-item questionnaire used to measure four socially aversive personality traits: subclinical psychopathy, narcissism, Machiavellianism, and sadism. Because psychological tools built in one language and culture don't always translate cleanly, researchers led by Pawel Debski adapted the SD4 for Polish speakers and tested it on 931 adults (average age about 35, roughly three-quarters women) recruited online. Using split-sample statistical testing, meaning the sample was divided so one half could generate a model and the other half could confirm it, the team compared several ways the four traits might fit together. A model that included both trait-specific scales and one broader underlying "dark personality" factor fit the data best. Most subscales showed acceptable reliability, and the sadism items in particular lined up well with an established sadism measure, supporting the tool's validity. However, the Machiavellianism subscale showed weaker internal consistency (alpha = .67), meaning its items didn't hang together as tightly as the other traits' items did. The authors conclude the Polish SD4 is usable as a brief dark-personality screener but say results from the Machiavellianism scale, and comparisons between men and women, should be interpreted cautiously. The sample was an online convenience sample with a gender imbalance and no formal back-translation check, which limits how confidently the findings generalize.
